sec.title: Background
sec.p: The onchocerciasis program in Chad is conducting several surveillance activities to verify the interruption of disease transmission and determine whether to stop the mass drug administration program that has been ongoing in the country since 1998.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Entomological surveillance was conducted from June 2021 to February 2022 in the onchocerciasis-persistent focus of Oulibangala, Chad.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 6962 Simulium spp. blackflies were collected near Oulibangala (n=5871) and Kaitia (n=1181). Vector blackflies were pooled and tested for Onchocerca volvulus DNA using O-150 polymerase chain reaction.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: No O. volvulus infections were detected, suggesting potential interruption of transmission in the area.
Keywords: Chad, Kaitia, onchocerciasis, Oulibangala, PCR O-150, transmission

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Onchocerciasis is a filarial disease targeted for elimination of transmission globally through mass drug administration of ivermectin to at-risk populations.1 In Chad, ivermectin treatment since 1998 has led to significant progress towards onchocerciasis elimination. The country was recently delineated into five operational transmission zones, with persistent hotspots identified in a single operational transmission zone.2 In 2014, the national onchocerciasis control program (PNLO) conducted an epidemiological evaluation using the skin snip method, which revealed prevalence rates of zero in the majority of the villages surveyed, except Oulibangala, which stood out with a prevalence of 2.02% (Figure 1), indicating ongoing transmission. Entomological assessments between 2011 and 2016 using O-150 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on vector blackflies collected near Oulibangala showed an infectivity rate of 3.65%, above the 0.05% threshold, confirming ongoing transmission. Following seven additional rounds of ivermectin treatment, vector blackflies were collected from Oulibangala and Kaitia in 2021 and 2022 and analysed using O-150 PCR to determine infectivity in the focus area. This article presents the results of these entomological surveys.

sec.title: Study sites
sec.p: The study was conducted from June 2021 to February 2022 in the villages of Oulibangala and Kaitia, located 12 km apart in the Baibokoum health district, Logone Oriental Province, Chad. Like all endemic areas, the two villages, situated along the Lim and Logone Rivers, respectively, continue to receive annual ivermectin treatments, conducted since 1998. One fly capture point was established near each village: in Oulibangala, 1 km from the village near a bridge over the Lim River, and in Katia, at the confluence of the Logone and Lim Rivers, approximately 2 km from the village.

sec.title: Capture and analysis of Simulium damnosum blackflies
sec.p: Blackflies were captured 1 day/week at the Oulibangala and Kaitia capture points from June 2021 to February 2022, using standard bulk collection methods from 07:00 h to 18:00 h. Specimens were preserved in 80% alcohol and sent to the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism/World Health Organization (WHO) molecular laboratory in Ouagadougou for analysis. Flies were morphologically identified according to the WHO criteria3 and tested using O-150 PCR.4 Pools of 200 Simulium heads were screened for Onchocerca volvulus DNA using PCR and O. volvulus-specific DNA probes. Infectivity rates and 95% confidence intervals were calculated using PoolScreen version 2.0. Since both sites fall within the same transmission zone, an overall infectivity rate was calculated and compared with the critical threshold defined by the WHO to assess ongoing transmission.1

sec.title: Simulium densities
sec.p: A total of 7020 vector blackflies were collected, with 5839 from Oulibangala and 1181 from Kaitia (Table 1). In Oulibangala, fly activity increased steadily from the lowest point in June, peaking in February with 1454 flies. High monthly captures were recorded from December through February (1075, 1427 and 1454, respectively), indicating intense vector presence during the dry season. At Kaitia, no flies were caught before August and collection rose gradually, also peaking in February (305 flies). These trends show a strong seasonal pattern, with vector densities increasing after the onset of rains and remaining high through the dry season. Persistent high biting rates, particularly near both capture points, pose a continued risk for onchocerciasis transmission, as elevated biting density correlates with increased transmission potential.3

sec.title: Infectivity rate and onchocerciasis transmission status
sec.p: All captured vector blackflies tested negative for O. volvulus infection, with an overall infectivity rate of 0.00% (95% confidence interval 0.00 to 0.02742), indicating interruption of transmission at the focal area. These findings align with dissection results reported by Mahamat et al.5 The observed onchocerciasis transmission interruption is likely due to an additional 7 y of treatment. However, the risk of reinfection remains, as the study area borders the Central African Republic and Cameroon, with which it shares endemic foci of onchocerciasis.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The results of this study indicate that interruption of transmission in the study area is likely and therefore suggest that the PNLO should begin stop mass drug administration assessments, in line with WHO guidelines, to evaluate whether transmission has been interrupted countrywide. Given the proximity to endemic areas in the Central African Republic and Cameroon, cross-border collaboration and synchronised surveillance efforts are recommended to mitigate the risk of reinfection.

sec.title: Ethical approval
sec.p: Chad’s national ethics committee gave its approval (n°037/PT/PM/MESRI/SE/SG/CNBT/SG/2023) for the implementation of field activities. All those involved in the capture of vector blackflies using the bulk capture method signed consent forms after being informed of the project’s activities. The consent forms were written in French and in the local language. The people involved in the study were trained in fly capture. To further reduce the risk of transmission, all study participants received ivermectin treatment as part of the national program’s mass distribution campaign.
